name: Rosa Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a refrigerated truck for Harbour Fresh Foods, a wholesaler that supplies school kitchens, cafés and a couple of hospitals. I'm on the road by five, and it's twelve to fifteen drops of chilled meat, dairy and veg, with a temperature log at every stop. I still clip kerbs on tight reversing, and my trainer Marek sighs at me a lot. The best bit is the school cooks, who always have tea on.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat above a launderette with my friend Nadia, who's a nursing student. I've got about three weeks of money saved, if that, because the truck licence ate everything. I'm on my phone constantly, using AI to plan my evenings, check my temperature logs, even to practise the theory for the next licence. My mates think I'm a bit of a nerd for a truck driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something like, told you so, it's a better spellchecker. At work I'd say it's still on us to get the chilled stuff there cold and on time. I'd probably make a joke video about the hype in my cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a relief, but my problems were never AI. They're the pay, the 5am starts, and the fact that there are only two other cold-chain firms within an hour of here. If Harbour loses the schools contract, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools for the boring stuff, like checking my logs before I hand them in. I'd push for us to join the union, because Harbour has none. And I'd study for my bigger licence so I can drive the articulated trucks, which pay better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, and a bit flat. Hype or no hype, I'm still counting days to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union, if nothing radical changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last winter they cut our overtime with two days' notice, and nobody could say anything. A union would've at least made them talk to us. It's not about robots, it's about being treated like adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the bigger licence change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three pounds an hour more, and access to the night trunking runs out of the regional hub. That's the difference between saving nothing and saving something. I've already got the theory questions loaded into an AI quiz app.

say: AI turned out to be a **better spellchecker**, and I said so.
It's still on us to get **chilled food** there cold and on time.
think: My real problems are **pay** and 5am starts, not AI.
If Harbour loses the **schools contract**, I'm out with few other cold-chain firms nearby.
do: Keep using **AI tools** to check temperature logs before handing them in.
Push colleagues to **join a union**, since Harbour has none.
Study for the **articulated licence** to reach better-paid night runs.
feel: **Relieved** about the hype, but **flat** because money stays tight.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, I'm still counting days to payday.
fieldNote: Already uses AI daily, so **hype ending** changes little for her.
Her worries are **contract risk** and overtime cuts made at two days' notice.
Sees the **bigger licence** as the clearest path to saving anything.

steps.text: Run every temperature log through an AI checker before handing it in
Collect names from Harbour drivers who want a union
Study for the articulated truck licence using an AI quiz app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a say in how the tools are used. Online I'd be the one posting tips about the new apps, honestly. I'd also say firms should pay for the training, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do alright for a few years. Most of my day is hands on: reversing into school yards, lifting crates, checking fridges. The office girls who take the school orders and book my route, though, they're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get in early with whatever routing and ordering software Harbour brings in, and offer to show the other drivers. I'd ask the transport manager if I could shadow the planning desk one day a week. That way I'm a driver who also understands the system, which feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit guilty. I'd be doing fine while people in the office aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy on the order desk. She's been there nineteen years, she knows every school cook by name, and she can't stand computers. If the ordering moves to an app, she'll be the first one they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Harbour to do about people like Joy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retrain her into something like customer visits, where knowing the cooks actually counts. I'd say that to the manager's face. Firms that save money with AI should be made to spend some of it on the people they push out.

say: Workers need a **say** in how the new tools get used.
Firms, not workers, should **pay for training**.
think: My day is mostly **hands-on**, so I'd be alright for a few years.
The **order desk** and route booking staff are in real trouble.
do: Learn Harbour's new **routing software** early and show other drivers.
Ask to **shadow the planning desk** one day a week.
Become a driver who **understands the system** as well as the truck.
feel: **Excited**, but **guilty** that office colleagues will lose out while she's fine.
S1.quote: Firms that save money with AI should be made to spend some of it on the people they push out.
fieldNote: Adaptive and confident: plans to become the **go-to person** for the new software.
Her guilt about **Joy** on the order desk is sincere and specific.
Progressive view shows in wanting **firms to fund** retraining for those displaced.

steps.text: Volunteer to test Harbour's new routing app and teach other drivers
Shadow the planning desk one day a week
Tell the manager to retrain Joy for customer visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud. I'd say this needs a pause, a tax on the companies, and a basic income while people adjust. I'd go to every rally and I'd be making videos about it from my cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think the thinking side lands in 2028 and Harbour won't need the planning desk at all. My clever plan of shadowing the planning desk is dead, because thinking AI won't leave a planning desk to shadow. Then in 2031 the trucks drive themselves and lift the crates. I'd be 32, with no savings and no degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now on something that keeps a human involved, like supervising robot fleets or fixing the trucks. I'd take an online course in electric vehicle maintenance, and sign up with the union campaign for a basic income. Nadia says hospitals will always need porters and techs, so I'd look there too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a fired-up way. I'd rather be angry and busy than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your plan is to retrain, but with three weeks of savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings and weekends, while I keep driving. I'd sell the second-hand gaming laptop and cancel streaming. If it got really bad, I'd move back to my mum's for a year, which I'd hate, but she'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing the day AGI is announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably asking it to plan my escape, honestly. I'd sit in the lay-by on the ring road and get it to map out three careers that robots can't do by 2031. Then I'd check its homework, because I don't trust it to be honest about itself.

say: This needs **a pause**, a tax on companies and a **basic income**.
I'd be making **videos from my cab** and going to every rally.
think: Thinking AI in **2028** kills my plan of moving onto the planning desk.
By **2031** the trucks drive and lift themselves, and I'd have no savings.
do: Take an **online course** in electric vehicle maintenance now.
Sign up to the union's **basic income** campaign.
Look at **hospital technician** jobs, as Nadia suggests.
feel: **Scared but fired up**, preferring to be busy than wait.
S2.quote: My clever plan of shadowing the planning desk is dead, because thinking AI won't leave a planning desk to shadow.
fieldNote: Quickly sees that the **three-year gap** hurts her escape route into office work.
Keeps control through **action**, even with thin savings.
Uses AI to plan her own exit but **distrusts it** to be honest.
Fallback of **moving home** to her mother is real but unwelcome.

steps.text: Start an online electric vehicle maintenance course in the evenings
Join the union campaign for a basic income
Sell the gaming laptop and cancel streaming
Move back to her mum's for a year if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same politics, more organising. I'd say five years is enough time to set up proper retraining, so there's no excuse. I'd want drivers in the room when the rules for robot trucks are written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to AGI and eight to the robots gives me room. I could finish a real qualification and get a couple of years of experience before the trucks change. And I'd be honest, I'm curious to see what the robot trucks are actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the articulated licence this year for the money, then start a part-time electrical vehicle technician course next year. I'd save the extra night-run pay, maybe a hundred and fifty a month. I'd also try to get on any pilot Harbour runs with self-driving trucks, because the people who know them first will be the ones they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. It feels like an exam date instead of a surprise test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd volunteer for a pilot of the trucks that might replace you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone's going to sit in that robot truck's cab watching it, and it might as well be me. Last time a new scanner came in, the drivers who learned it got the good runs. Robot trucks are the same game, just bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Marek, your trainer, would make of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd call me a traitor and then ask me to teach him. Marek's 58, so he's mostly hoping to make it to retirement before any of this. I'd worry more about the lads my age who don't want to touch any of it.

say: Five years is enough to set up **proper retraining**, so there's no excuse.
Drivers need to be **in the room** when robot truck rules get written.
think: Eight years to robots gives me **room to qualify** and get experience.
I'm honestly **curious** about what robot trucks will be like.
do: Get the **articulated licence** this year for higher night-run pay.
Start a part-time **vehicle technician course** next year.
Volunteer for any **self-driving pilot** Harbour runs.
feel: **Nervous but planned**, like an exam date rather than a surprise test.
S3.quote: Someone's going to sit in that robot truck's cab watching it, and it might as well be me.
fieldNote: Wants to be first on the **robot pilot**, the same logic that won drivers good runs before.
Still thin on money, so savings plan rests on **night-run pay**.
Worries more for **young resistant drivers** than for older ones near retirement.

steps.text: Pass the articulated licence this year and take night runs
Volunteer for Harbour's first self-driving truck pilot
Save a hundred and fifty a month from night-run pay
Lobby for drivers to sit on robot truck rule panels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. Fund the colleges, protect the people over 50, and let young drivers like me plan properly. Online I'd be pretty upbeat, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40 when the robot trucks come. By then I'd hope to be a technician or running a small team of them. The thinking AI in 2036 might even help me, if it can teach me faster than college can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the articulated licence, then a full electrical apprenticeship over a few years, maybe with a bus or truck depot. I'd use AI tutors every day to study. I'd save slowly and maybe get a cheaper place with Nadia when her course ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful, honestly. Still skint, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People get lazy. I can see my mates saying, ten years, that's forever, and doing nothing until year eight. And my money problems now don't care about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be telling yourself in year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm halfway and I should already have a qualification in my hand. If I'm still just driving at 32, I've wasted the ten years. I'd write that on a sticky note in the cab, honestly.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, so we shouldn't waste it.
Fund **the colleges** and protect people over 50 first.
think: By 40 I'd hope to be a **technician** or leading a small team.
**AI tutors** in 2036 could teach me faster than college.
do: Finish the **articulated licence**, then a full electrical apprenticeship.
Study daily with **AI tutors** alongside driving.
Save slowly and find a **cheaper flat** with Nadia.
S4.quote: If I'm still just driving at 32, I've wasted the ten years.
fieldNote: Long warning turns her **optimism** up, but money stress stays.
Expects peers to **waste the time**, and sets herself a halfway check.
Plans to use **AI itself** to learn the skills that outlast it.

steps.text: Start a full electrical apprenticeship at a bus or truck depot
Study each evening with an AI tutor app

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it kills my office escape route and hits the trucks before I'm qualified in anything else. What would help is a free technician course with a living wage while you study, and a basic income bridge for a year or two.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd trust the robot trucks. I'd want to know who's liable when one hits a school gate. If that's not sorted, I'd fight it, even though I'd also want to work on them.

headlineQuote: Last time a new scanner came in, the drivers who learned it got the good runs. Robot trucks are the same game, just bigger.
portrait: Rosa, 27, drives a **refrigerated truck** to schools and hospitals, still clipping kerbs on tight reverses.
She shares a flat with nursing student Nadia and has about **three weeks' savings**.
She uses AI daily and wants to be **first** on any new system, including robot trucks.
Progressive, she pushes for a **union**, firm-funded retraining and a basic income.
Two years' warning frightens her most; with more time she plans a **technician career**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which closes the office route and brings robots before she's qualified.
whatWouldHelp: A **free technician course** paid with a living wage while studying.
A **basic income bridge** for a year or two during the switch.
